messages.content:
Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the welcome page new engineers see on their first day at a software company. Around 250 words.

output:
Welcome. You're joining a company that builds software people rely on, and today you get access, a laptop, and a lot of unfamiliar context. That's normal. Nobody expects you to understand the whole system by Friday.

Your first two weeks are for orientation, not output. Set up your environment, get your accounts working, and read through the onboarding docs linked in your calendar invite. You'll be paired with a buddy from your team who can answer the questions that feel too small to ask in a group channel — use them.

By the end of week one, expect to have your development environment running and your first pull request merged, even if it's a small one. Small changes teach you the review process, the deploy pipeline, and who to ask when something breaks. By the end of month one, you'll have met your skip-level manager, sat in on a customer call or support rotation if your team does one, and picked up your first real project.

Ask questions in the open. If you're stuck for more than twenty minutes, post in your team channel instead of grinding alone — someone has hit the same wall before. Code review comments here are about the code, not you; take what's useful and move on.

Your manager will set up a 30-60-90 day check-in schedule with you in your first week. Bring questions to those meetings, including ones about how your role or team might change.

Look around. The people who onboarded you were new once too, and the documentation you'll edit next month is the same documentation that's confusing you today. Fix it when you find the gap.
